decision.explanation: The slope is y′(π)/x′(π). Since sin(π)=0 and cos(π)=−1, y′(π)=−ln(π) and x′(π)=−1/π. Thus the slope is π ln(π), option b.

after.name: Question 1
after.problem:
Find the slope of the tangent line to the polar curve $r=\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta $, at $\theta =\pi $,  given that 

$$
{y}^{′}(\theta )=\frac{1}{\theta }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,\,{x}^{′}(\theta )=\frac{1}{\theta }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$
after.worked_solution:
To find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ we use the rule for differentiating parametric equations:

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )}
$$

Evaluating the numerator and denominator at $\theta =\pi ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(\pi ) & =\frac{1}{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi +\operatorname{ln}⁡\pi \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi  \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }\cdot 0+\operatorname{ln}⁡\pi \cdot (-1) \\  & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡\pi ,\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(\pi ) & =\frac{1}{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi -\operatorname{ln}⁡\pi \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\pi  \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }\cdot (-1)-\operatorname{ln}⁡\pi \cdot 0 \\  & =-\frac{1}{\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Hence, the slope of the tangent line is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{\theta =\pi } & =\frac{{y}^{′}(\pi )}{{x}^{′}(\pi )} \\  & =\frac{-\operatorname{ln}⁡\pi }{(-\frac{1}{\pi })} \\  & =\pi \operatorname{ln}⁡\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

To find dydx, we use the rule for differentiating parametric equations:

dydx=y′(θ)x′(θ)

Evaluating the numerator and denominator at θ=π, we have y′(π)=1πsin⁡π+ln⁡π⋅cos⁡π=1π⋅0+ln⁡π⋅(−1)=−ln⁡π, and x′(π)=1πcos⁡π−ln⁡π⋅sin⁡π=1π⋅(−1)−ln⁡π⋅0=−1π.

after.name: Question 2
after.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14068032/assets/70c737e1fbbf63b3551763e48f4d7a956ffcc04ff68cced4f813b28e87630eb3.png)

For the polar curve $r=\frac{{e}^{2\theta }}{2\pi },$ calculate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ as a function of $\theta .$

| $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ | $=$ | {{field-1}} |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  |  | $2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ |
after.worked_solution:
To find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ we use the formula for differentiating parametric curves:

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )}
$$

First, we recall that to convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta 
$$

Using the fact that $r=\frac{{e}^{2\theta }}{2\pi },$ we get

$$
x=\frac{{e}^{2\theta }}{2\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=\frac{{e}^{2\theta }}{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

To compute our derivative, we first need to calculate ${x}^{′}(\theta )$ and ${y}^{′}(\theta ).$ 

- First, we compute the derivative of $x$ with respect to $\theta $ using the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(\theta ) & ={(\frac{{e}^{2\theta }}{2\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{′} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\pi }{({e}^{2\theta }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{′} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\pi }[({e}^{2\theta })^{′}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{e}^{2\theta }\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{′}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2\pi }[2{e}^{2\theta }\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{e}^{2\theta }\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )] \\  & =\frac{1}{2\pi }[2{e}^{2\theta }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -{e}^{2\theta }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ] \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2\theta }}{2\pi }(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\end{aligned}
$$

- Then, we compute the derivative of $y$ with respect to $\theta $ using the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(\theta ) & ={(\frac{{e}^{2\theta }}{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{′} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\pi }{({e}^{2\theta }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{′} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\pi }[({e}^{2\theta })^{′}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +{e}^{2\theta }\cdot (\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{′}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2\pi }[2{e}^{2\theta }\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +{e}^{2\theta }\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )] \\  & =\frac{1}{2\pi }[2{e}^{2\theta }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +{e}^{2\theta }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ] \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2\theta }}{2\pi }(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )} \\  & =\frac{\frac{{e}^{2\theta }}{2\pi }(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}{\frac{{e}^{2\theta }}{2\pi }(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )} \\  & =\frac{2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2

For the polar curve r=e2θ2π, calculate dydx as a function of θ.
dydx
=
2sin(θ)−cos(θ)
2cos⁡θ−sin⁡θ
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

To find dydx, we use the formula for differentiating parametric curves: dydx=y′(θ)x′(θ)

First, we recall that to convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use x=rcos⁡θ,y=rsin⁡θ

Using the fact that r=e2θ2π, we get x=e2θ2πcos⁡θ,y=e2θ2πsin⁡θ.

To compute our derivative, we first need to calculate x′(θ) and y′(θ).

  • First, we compute the derivative of x with respect to θ using the product rule: x′(θ)=(e2θ2πcos⁡θ)′=12π(e2θcos⁡θ)′=12π[(e2θ)′⋅cos⁡θ+e2θ⋅(cos⁡θ)′]=12π[2e2θ⋅cos⁡θ+e2θ⋅(−sin⁡θ)]=12π[2e2θcos⁡θ−e2θsin⁡θ]=e2θ2π(2cos⁡θ−sin⁡θ)

  • Then, we compute the derivative of y with respect to θ using the product rule: y′(θ)=(e2θ2πsin⁡θ)′=12π(e2θsin⁡θ)′=12π[(e2θ)′⋅sin⁡θ+e2θ⋅(sin⁡θ)′]=12π[2e2θ⋅sin⁡θ+e2θ⋅(cos⁡θ)]=12π[2e2θsin⁡θ+e2θcos⁡θ]=e2θ2π(2sin⁡θ+cos⁡θ)

Therefore, dydx=y′(θ)x′(θ)=e2θ2π(2sin⁡θ+cos⁡θ)e2θ2π(2cos⁡θ−sin⁡θ)=2sin⁡θ+cos⁡θ2cos⁡θ−sin⁡θ.

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms the numerator is 2 sin(θ)+cos(θ): the product rule gives y′=r(2 sin(θ)+cos(θ)) and x′=r(2 cos(θ)−sin(θ)). The deliberately submitted minus-sign expression is incorrect; the earlier correct answer remains valid.

\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(\theta ) & ={(\frac{{e}^{2\theta }}{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{′} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\pi }{({e}^{2\theta }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{′} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\pi }[({e}^{2\theta })^{′}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +{e}^{2\theta }\cdot (\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{′}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2\pi }[2{e}^{2\theta }\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +{e}^{2\theta }\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )] \\  & =\frac{1}{2\pi }[2{e}^{2\theta }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +{e}^{2\theta }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ] \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2\theta }}{2\pi }(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )} \\  & =\frac{\frac{{e}^{2\theta }}{2\pi }(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}{\frac{{e}^{2\theta }}{2\pi }(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )} \\  & =\frac{2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 4
after.worked_solution:
To find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ we use the formula for differentiating parametric curves:

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )}
$$

First, we recall that to convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

Using the fact that $r=22,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =22\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=22\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Calculating the necessary derivatives, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(\theta ) & =-22\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,{y}^{′}(\theta )=22\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{22\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{-22\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta } \\  & =-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta } \\  & =-\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$
